entries.term: zero article with abstract nouns: Happiness is …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Abstract nouns used in a general sense take no article (*Happiness is …*, *Life is short*); *the* appears when the noun is made specific (*the happiness of children*).
entries.usage: A very common error for learners whose languages use an article here, such as French, Spanish, German or Greek. The noun becomes specific through an *of*-phrase, a relative clause or the context (*the history of Japan*, *the life she wanted*). Some general nouns usually keep *the* in fixed uses: *the environment*, *the economy*, *the future*.
entries.pattern: Ø + abstract noun (general) / the + abstract noun + of-phrase or clause (specific)
examples: **Patience** isn't one of my strengths, especially in traffic.
They say **money** can't buy **happiness**, but it certainly helps with the rent.
**Trust** takes years to build and only seconds to lose.

drill.sentence: {{The history}} of this old building is more interesting than you'd think.
drill.hint: General or specific? Complete with history: ___ of this old building is more interesting than you'd think.

mistake.wrong: The life is too short to stay angry.
mistake.right: Life is too short to stay angry.
mistake.why: In a general statement, an abstract noun takes no article.

entries.term: generic plural without the: Dogs are loyal
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A plural noun with no article talks about a whole class in general: *Dogs are loyal* means dogs in general; *The dogs are loyal* means particular dogs.
entries.usage: The most common way to make general statements in both speech and writing. Adding *the* makes the noun refer to a group the listener can identify (*The dogs next door bark all night*). Uncountable nouns work the same way (*Coffee keeps me awake*).
entries.pattern: Ø + plural noun (general) / the + plural noun (specific group)
examples: **Cats** are generally much more independent than **dogs**.
**Teenagers** need more sleep than most parents realize.
I've never really been into **horror movies**, even as a teenager.

drill.sentence: {{Bees}} are essential for growing fruit and vegetables.
drill.hint: Correct the article for a general statement: The bees are essential for growing fruit and vegetables.

mistake.wrong: The women live longer than the men on average.
mistake.right: Women live longer than men on average.
mistake.why: In a general statement, a plural noun takes no article; *the women* would mean a specific group.

entries.term: a number of vs. the number of
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *A number of* + plural noun means *several* or *many* and takes a plural verb; *the number of* + plural noun refers to the number itself and takes a singular verb.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and conversation. *A number of* is a slightly vague, polite way to say *several* (*A number of people have asked …*). With *the number of*, the verb agrees with *number*: *The number of cases is rising*.
entries.pattern: a number of + plural noun + plural verb / the number of + plural noun + singular verb
examples: **A number of** neighbors **have** complained about the noise from the new bar.
**The number of** cars on our street **has** doubled since the new school opened.
**A growing number of** young families **are** choosing to rent instead of buy.

drill.sentence: A number of parents {{have}} asked the school to start classes later.
drill.hint: Choose has or have: A number of parents ___ asked the school to start classes later.

mistake.wrong: The number of accidents are increasing.
mistake.right: The number of accidents is increasing.
mistake.why: The subject is *number*, so the verb is singular; only *a number of* takes a plural verb.

entries.term: singular they: Someone left their phone
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *They, them, their* can refer to one person whose gender is unknown or not important, or to a person who uses *they* as their pronoun: *Someone left their phone.*
entries.usage: Normal in speech for centuries and now accepted in writing by major American style guides such as AP and APA. It is much smoother than *he or she*. The verb stays plural even for one person (*they are*, *they were*).
entries.pattern: someone / anyone / every + noun / a person … + they / them / their (+ plural verb)
examples: Someone left **their** umbrella in the break room.
If a customer complains, **they** usually get a free dessert.
Alex said **they're** running late, so let's start without **them**.

drill.sentence: Every guest should bring {{their}} own towel to the pool party.
drill.hint: Replace his or her: Every guest should bring his or her own towel to the pool party.

mistake.wrong: Ask the new student if they has a laptop.
mistake.right: Ask the new student if they have a laptop.
mistake.why: Singular *they* still takes a plural verb: *they have*, *they are*, *they were*.

entries.term: collective nouns in American English: The team is …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In American English, collective nouns like *team, family, company, staff* and *band* usually take a singular verb (*The team is …*); British English often uses a plural verb (*The team are …*).
entries.usage: American editors and most speakers treat the group as one unit (*The committee has decided*). A later pronoun is often *they*, even in US English (*The team is happy with their result*), although editors prefer *its*. Some nouns are always plural (*the police are*), and plural team names take plural verbs (*the Yankees are*).
entries.pattern: the team / family / company / staff / band + is / has (US)
examples: **The team is** playing its last home game of the season tonight.
**My family has** lived in this town for four generations.
**The company is** cutting jobs again, so everyone's nervous.

drill.sentence: The band {{is}} going on tour across the Midwest next spring.
drill.hint: Use American agreement: The band ___ going on tour across the Midwest next spring.

mistake.wrong: The police is investigating the robbery.
mistake.right: The police are investigating the robbery.
mistake.why: *Police* is always plural, in American English too; the singular verb is for nouns like *team* and *family*.

entries.term: uncountable nouns: research, feedback, advice (no plural)
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Nouns like *research, feedback, advice, information, equipment, furniture* and *luggage* are uncountable in English: they take no plural *-s* and no *a/an*.
entries.usage: Use *some, much, a lot of*, or a counting word: *a piece of advice*, *a study* (for one piece of research), *a comment* (for one piece of feedback). Many of these nouns are countable in other languages, so learners from many backgrounds add *-s*. The verb is singular (*The feedback was helpful*).
entries.pattern: Ø / some / much / a lot of + advice / feedback / research / information + singular verb; a piece of + noun
examples: My grandfather gave me one great piece of **advice**: never sign anything you haven't read.
Thanks for the **feedback** on my presentation; it was really helpful.
How much **luggage** are you bringing on the trip?

drill.sentence: Can you give me some {{advice}} on buying a used car?
drill.hint: Correct the noun: Can you give me some advices on buying a used car?

mistake.wrong: We got many feedbacks from our customers.
mistake.right: We got a lot of feedback from our customers.
mistake.why: *Feedback* is uncountable: no plural and no *many*; use *a lot of* or *much*.

entries.term: most people vs. most of the people vs. the most
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Most* + noun means the majority in general (*most people*); *most of the* + noun means the majority of a specific group (*most of the people at the party*); *the most* means the largest amount (*She got the most votes*).
entries.usage: *The most of people* and *most of people* are common errors for learners from many languages. *Most of* needs a determiner, a pronoun or a name after it (*most of the, most of my, most of them, most of Texas*). *The most* is a superlative, not a word for a majority.
entries.pattern: most + noun (general) / most of + the / my / these + noun (specific) / the most + noun (largest amount)
examples: **Most people** I know would rather text than call.
**Most of the** guests left before midnight, but a few stayed to help clean up.
The kid who sold **the most** cookies won a free week at summer camp.

drill.sentence: {{Most of the people}} in my building are retired teachers.
drill.hint: Correct the error, keeping of: Most of people in my building are retired teachers.

mistake.wrong: The most of my friends are married now.
mistake.right: Most of my friends are married now.
mistake.why: Use *most of* + *my / the / these* for a majority; *the most* is only for the largest amount.

entries.term: agreement with the head noun: The quality of the products is …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: The verb agrees with the head (main) noun of the subject, not with the noun closest to it: *The quality of the products is …*
entries.usage: Long subjects with *of*-phrases, relative clauses or other modifiers make this easy to get wrong, for native speakers too. Find the main noun first (*quality*, not *products*). Quantity words like *a lot of*, *the majority of* and fractions are the exception: there, the noun after *of* decides.
entries.pattern: head noun + (of / in / with … + other noun) + verb agreeing with the head noun
examples: **The quality** of the photos **is** much better on the new phone.
**The list** of things I need to do before the trip **keeps** getting longer.
**One** of my neighbors **has** three German shepherds.

drill.sentence: The cost of all these repairs {{is}} higher than the car is worth.
drill.hint: Choose is or are: The cost of all these repairs ___ higher than the car is worth.

mistake.wrong: The price of these shoes are ridiculous.
mistake.right: The price of these shoes is ridiculous.
mistake.why: The verb agrees with *price*, not with *shoes*, the noun closest to it.

entries.term: there's + plural noun in speech: There's a lot of people
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In casual speech, many native speakers use *there's* before a plural noun (*There's a lot of people here*, *There's two options*); in writing, *there are* is expected.
entries.usage: Extremely common in everyday conversation, especially with *a lot of*, numbers and lists, and most listeners don't notice it. The full form *there is* + plural noun sounds much more wrong than the contraction. In emails, essays and formal talks, use *there are*.
entries.pattern: there's + plural noun (casual speech) / there are + plural noun (writing)
examples: **There's a lot of people** waiting outside; I think the doors open at eight.
Honestly, **there's two ways** we can do this, and neither one is great.
**There's** some cookies in the jar if you're hungry.

drill.sentence: {{There are}} three issues we need to discuss before Friday's meeting.
drill.hint: Make it suitable for writing: There's three issues we need to discuss before Friday's meeting.

mistake.wrong: There is many reasons to visit Chicago.
mistake.right: There are many reasons to visit Chicago.
mistake.why: The full form *there is* before a plural noun sounds wrong even to native ears; write *there are*.

entries.term: between you and me (not I)
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After a preposition like *between, for, with* or *to*, use object pronouns: *between you and me*, *for Sarah and me*; *between you and I* is a hypercorrection.
entries.usage: Many native speakers say *between you and I* or *for John and I*, because they were taught that *me and John* is wrong and now avoid *me* everywhere. It is common even among educated speakers, but editors treat it as an error and many listeners notice it. Quick test: remove the other person (*for me*, not *for I*).
entries.pattern: preposition + you / him / her / name + and + me
examples: **Between you and me**, I don't think he's going to last long in that job.
Thanks for having **my wife and me** over last night.
Grandma left the lake house to **my brother and me**.

drill.sentence: The waiter brought a free dessert for Sarah and {{me}}.
drill.hint: Correct the pronoun: The waiter brought a free dessert for Sarah and I.

mistake.wrong: Just between you and I, the party was a disaster.
mistake.right: Just between you and me, the party was a disaster.
mistake.why: *Between* is a preposition, so it takes the object form *me*.

entries.term: pronoun case in compound subjects: He and I went (not me and him)
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In a subject, use subject pronouns: *He and I went*, *My sister and I live …*; *Me and him went* is very informal.
entries.usage: *Me and him went* is extremely common in casual American speech, but many listeners consider it nonstandard, and it is avoided in writing. Politeness puts *I* last (*my wife and I*). Quick test: remove the other person (*I went*, not *me went*).
entries.pattern: he / she / they / name + and + I + verb
examples: **My brother and I** used to fight over the TV remote every night.
**She and her husband** just bought a small farm in Vermont.
**He and I** have been friends since kindergarten.

drill.sentence: {{Jake and I}} drove to Nashville for the weekend.
drill.hint: Make it correct for writing: Me and Jake drove to Nashville for the weekend.

mistake.wrong: Him and his wife are moving to Florida next year.
mistake.right: He and his wife are moving to Florida next year.
mistake.why: In a subject, use subject pronouns: *he and his wife*, *she and I*.

entries.term: compound adjective with a number: a ten-minute walk
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A number + noun used as an adjective before another noun is hyphenated, and the noun stays singular: *a ten-minute walk*, *a three-year-old girl*, *a 40-hour week*.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing for time, distance, age, money and size. The noun is singular because it acts as an adjective (*a two-hour meeting*, not *a two-hours meeting*); after a verb, the normal plural returns (*The walk takes ten minutes*). Ages follow the same rule: *a five-year-old*, but *She is five years old*.
entries.pattern: a + number-noun (singular, hyphenated) + noun
examples: The hotel is a **ten-minute walk** from the beach.
We just adopted a **two-year-old** rescue dog from the shelter.
She works **twelve-hour shifts** at the hospital three days a week.

drill.sentence: It was an exhausting {{five-hour}} flight, and the baby cried the whole time.
drill.hint: Use a compound adjective: The flight lasted five hours and was exhausting, and the baby cried the whole time.

mistake.wrong: We're planning a two-weeks vacation in Mexico.
mistake.right: We're planning a two-week vacation in Mexico.
mistake.why: In a compound adjective before a noun, the noun stays singular.

entries.term: every other / every few: every other day
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Every other* + singular noun means *every second one*: *every other day* is one day yes, one day no. *Every few* + plural noun means *at short, regular intervals*: *every few minutes*.
entries.usage: Common in all registers. Note the number: *every other week* (singular), but *every few weeks* and *every two weeks* (plural). *Every other* can also mean *all the others* (*Every other kid in class has a phone*), so the context decides.
entries.pattern: every other + singular noun / every few, two, three + plural noun
examples: I run **every other day** and do yoga on the days in between.
The bus comes **every few minutes** during rush hour.
We get together with my college roommates **every other summer**.

drill.sentence: Water the plant {{every other day}} in summer and once a week in winter.
drill.hint: Rewrite with every: Water the plant on alternate days in summer and once a week in winter.

mistake.wrong: My son sees his dad every other weeks.
mistake.right: My son sees his dad every other week.
mistake.why: *Every other* takes a singular noun; only *every few* and *every two* take a plural.

entries.term: quite a few / quite a bit (= many / much)
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Quite a few* + plural noun means *a fairly large number*, and *quite a bit (of)* means *a fairly large amount*, despite the words *few* and *bit*.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation and informal writing; it is a relaxed, slightly understated way to say *many* or *a lot*. *Quite a bit* also works with comparatives and verbs (*quite a bit colder*, *He travels quite a bit*). Don't confuse it with *a few*, which means some, or *few*, which means not many.
entries.pattern: quite a few + plural noun / quite a bit of + uncountable noun / quite a bit + comparative
examples: **Quite a few** of my friends have moved to Austin recently.
Fixing the roof is going to cost **quite a bit** more than we planned.
She's put on **quite a bit of** muscle since she started lifting.

drill.sentence: There were {{quite a few}} people at the farmers market this morning.
drill.hint: Say it casually, using few: There were many people at the farmers market this morning.

mistake.wrong: Quite a few people came, so the room was almost empty.
mistake.right: Only a few people came, so the room was almost empty.
mistake.why: *Quite a few* means a fairly large number; for a small number, say *only a few* or *not many*.

entries.term: a couple + plural without of (US informal): a couple weeks
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In informal American English, *of* is often dropped after *a couple*: *a couple weeks* and *a couple bucks* mean *a couple of weeks* and *a couple of dollars*.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech and casual writing; British speakers notice it as American. In careful writing, use *a couple of*. In both forms, *a couple* often means *two or a few*, not exactly two.
entries.pattern: a couple (of) + plural noun
examples: I'll be out of town for **a couple weeks** in July.
Can you lend me **a couple bucks** for parking?
We met **a couple years** ago at a friend's barbecue.

drill.sentence: I'll call you back in {{a couple minutes}}; I'm just pulling into the garage.
drill.hint: Say it the casual American way (drop one word): I'll call you back in a couple of minutes; I'm just pulling into the garage.

mistake.wrong: I need a couple day off after the move.
mistake.right: I need a couple days off after the move.
mistake.why: Even without *of*, the noun after *a couple* stays plural.

entries.term: as many as / as much as + number
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Stresses that a number or amount is surprisingly large: *As many as 500 people showed up* means 500, which is a lot.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and speech, often with an estimate or an upper limit. Use *as many as* with countable nouns and *as much as* with money, percentages and uncountable amounts (*as much as $500*, *as much as a foot of snow*). The opposite emphasis is *as few as* or *as little as* (*for as little as $5*).
entries.pattern: as many as + number + plural noun / as much as + amount
examples: **As many as** 20,000 fans lined the streets for the championship parade.
Prices at the airport can be **as much as** 50 percent higher than downtown.
Some nights the baby wakes up **as many as** five times.

drill.sentence: The storm could bring {{as much as}} a foot of snow to the mountains.
drill.hint: Stress that the amount is surprisingly large: The storm could bring up to a foot of snow to the mountains.

mistake.wrong: As much as 300 people were evacuated.
mistake.right: As many as 300 people were evacuated.
mistake.why: *People* are countable, so use *as many as*; *as much as* is for amounts like money or snow.

entries.term: much in affirmative sentences: There is much to do
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In positive statements, *much* as a quantifier sounds formal or literary; in speech people say *a lot of* or *lots of*: *There's a lot to do*.
entries.usage: *Much* is normal in questions and negatives (*Not much*, *How much …?*) and after *too, so, as* and *very* (*too much*, *so much*). Without those words, positive *much* appears mainly in formal writing (*Much has been written about …*). *Much of* + *the / this* is less formal and is common in news and speech too.
entries.pattern: much (+ uncountable noun) in positive statements (formal) / a lot (of) in speech
examples: **Much** has changed in this neighborhood since I was a kid.
There is **much** to admire in her latest novel, despite its slow start.
Officials say **much** of the flood damage could have been prevented.

drill.sentence: There is {{much}} to learn from the way they handled the crisis.
drill.hint: Make it formal: There is a lot to learn from the way they handled the crisis.

mistake.wrong: I drank much coffee this morning.
mistake.right: I drank a lot of coffee this morning.
mistake.why: In a positive spoken sentence, *much* + noun sounds wrong; use *a lot of*, or keep *much* for questions, negatives and *too much*.

entries.term: generic the + singular: The smartphone changed …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *The* + singular countable noun can refer to a whole class, especially inventions, species and musical instruments: *The smartphone changed how we live.*
entries.usage: Typical of formal or semi-formal writing, documentaries and lectures; in conversation, the plural without *the* is more common (*Smartphones changed …*). It is the normal form for statements about a whole kind, such as an invention or a species (*Who invented the telephone?*). *A* + noun can describe a typical member, but not the kind as a whole.
entries.pattern: the + singular countable noun (= the whole class)
examples: **The smartphone** has completely changed the way people date.
Most people think Edison invented **the light bulb**, but the story is more complicated.
**The bald eagle** was once an endangered species in the United States.

drill.sentence: {{The printing press}} changed European history forever.
drill.hint: Rewrite about the invention as a whole, with the + singular: Printing presses changed European history forever.

mistake.wrong: A computer has changed the way we work.
mistake.right: The computer has changed the way we work.
mistake.why: *A computer* means one example; to talk about the invention as a whole, use *the computer* or *computers*.

entries.term: the + adjective: the rich, the unemployed
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *The* + adjective refers to a whole group of people with that quality and takes a plural verb: *The rich are getting richer.*
entries.usage: Common in news, essays and speeches (*the rich, the young, the injured, the unemployed*). The adjective never takes *-s*, and for one person you add a noun (*an unemployed neighbor*); style guides such as AP and APA now prefer *homeless people* and *older adults* to *the homeless* and *the elderly*. Nationality words in *-sh*, *-ch* and *-ese* work the same way (*the French*).
entries.pattern: the + adjective (= people who are …) + plural verb
examples: Fashion trends often start with **the young** and slowly spread to everyone else.
Several of **the injured were** flown to the hospital by helicopter.
The city runs a free job training program for **the unemployed**.

drill.sentence: Malibu has long been a playground for {{the rich and famous}}.
drill.hint: Shorten with the + adjective: Malibu has long been a playground for people who are rich and famous.

mistake.wrong: The rich is getting richer.
mistake.right: The rich are getting richer.
mistake.why: *The* + adjective means a group of people, so it takes a plural verb.

entries.term: a / an with an uncountable + adjective: a good education
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Some uncountable nouns take *a/an* when an adjective or an *of*-phrase describes a particular kind: *a good education*, *a deep knowledge of*, *a healthy respect for*.
entries.usage: Common with *education, knowledge, understanding, respect, interest, love* and *fear*, and with some qualities (*a quiet confidence*). The noun still has no plural, and without the adjective the article usually goes away (*Education matters*). Nouns like *advice, information, news* and *furniture* never take *a*, even with an adjective.
entries.pattern: a / an + adjective + uncountable noun (education, knowledge, understanding, respect …)
examples: Her parents worked two jobs so she could get **a good education**.
He has **a deep knowledge** of Civil War history.
Growing up near the ocean gave me **a healthy respect** for the water.

drill.sentence: She has {{an}} excellent understanding of how small businesses work.
drill.hint: Add the missing article: She has excellent understanding of how small businesses work.

mistake.wrong: That's a great news!
mistake.right: That's great news!
mistake.why: *News* is uncountable and never takes *a*, even with an adjective; for one item, say *a piece of news*.

entries.term: countable and uncountable senses: experience vs. an experience
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Some nouns change meaning when they become countable: *experience* (skill gained over time) vs. *an experience* (one event); also *time / a time*, *room / a room*, *paper / a paper*.
entries.usage: Very common in job interviews, résumés and storytelling: *five years of experience*, but *an amazing experience*. Saying *I have an experience in sales* sounds like one event, not job knowledge. Choose the form by asking whether you mean a general quality or one separate thing.
entries.pattern: experience (uncountable: skill) / an experience, experiences (countable: events)
examples: She has ten years of **experience** in emergency medicine.
Swimming with dolphins in Hawaii was **an unforgettable experience**.
We had **a great time** at your wedding, and the food was amazing.

drill.sentence: Do you have any {{experience}} working with young children?
drill.hint: Countable or uncountable? (job skill) Do you have any ___ working with young children?

mistake.wrong: I have an experience in project management.
mistake.right: I have experience in project management.
mistake.why: Job knowledge is uncountable *experience*; *an experience* is a single event.

entries.term: none of + singular or plural verb
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *None of* + plural noun can take a singular or a plural verb: *None of my friends has / have a car.* Both are correct.
entries.usage: The plural verb is more common in speech and in most modern writing; the singular sounds more formal and careful. With an uncountable noun, the verb is always singular (*None of the money was spent*). The idea that *none* must be singular is a myth, although some editors still prefer it.
entries.pattern: none of + plural noun + plural verb (common) / singular verb (formal); none of + uncountable noun + singular verb
examples: **None of** my friends **have** kids yet, so I'll be the first.
**None of** the proposals **was** approved by the city council.
**None of** the food **was** wasted; the kids finished everything.

drill.sentence: None of the information in the brochure {{was}} up to date.
drill.hint: Choose was or were (uncountable noun): None of the information in the brochure ___ up to date.

mistake.wrong: None of my friends don't have a car.
mistake.right: None of my friends have a car.
mistake.why: *None* is already negative, so the verb stays positive.

entries.term: each / every + singular verb: Each of them has …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Each* and *every* take a singular verb, even in *each of* + plural noun: *Each of them has a key.*
entries.usage: Common in all registers. After *each of*, the noun is plural but the verb stays singular (*Each of the rooms has a view*); *every* is followed by a singular noun (*Every room has a view*). When *each* comes after a plural subject, the verb is plural (*They each have a key*).
entries.pattern: each / every + singular noun + singular verb / each of + plural noun + singular verb / plural subject + each + plural verb
examples: **Each of** the kids **has** their own room in the new house.
**Every** house on our street **has** a big front porch.
My brothers **each have** a different opinion about what Dad should do.

drill.sentence: Each of the apartments {{has}} its own washer and dryer.
drill.hint: Choose has or have: Each of the apartments ___ its own washer and dryer.

mistake.wrong: Every students needs a laptop for this class.
mistake.right: Every student needs a laptop for this class.
mistake.why: *Every* takes a singular noun and a singular verb.

entries.term: neither of + plural noun: Neither of them is / are
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Neither of* + plural noun can take a singular verb (formal, traditional) or a plural verb (common in speech): *Neither of them is / are ready.*
entries.usage: In conversation and informal writing, the plural verb is normal; careful writers and exams prefer the singular. The noun after *neither of* is always plural (*neither of the options*), while *neither* without *of* takes a singular noun and verb (*Neither option is perfect*).
entries.pattern: neither of + plural noun / pronoun + is (formal) / are (common); neither + singular noun + singular verb
examples: **Neither of** my parents **is** very good with technology.
**Neither of** us **are** big fans of camping, so let's book a cabin.
**Neither** restaurant **was** open after ten, so we ended up getting pizza.

drill.sentence: Neither of my brothers {{lives}} nearby, so I only see them on holidays.
drill.hint: Use the formal singular verb: Neither of my brothers ___ (live) nearby, so I only see them on holidays.

mistake.wrong: Neither of the answer is correct.
mistake.right: Neither of the answers is correct.
mistake.why: After *neither of*, the noun is plural; only *neither* without *of* takes a singular noun (*neither answer*).

entries.term: either … or / neither … nor agreement
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: When two subjects are joined by *either … or* or *neither … nor*, the verb agrees with the one closer to it: *Neither the kids nor their father was home.*
entries.usage: This is the rule in careful writing; in speech, people often use a plural verb anyway. Many writers put the plural subject second, so the verb can be plural and sound natural (*Neither the father nor the kids were home*). The same rule applies to pronouns (*Either you or Jake has to stay*).
entries.pattern: either / neither + A + or / nor + B + verb agreeing with B
examples: **Either** my mom **or** my sisters **are** picking us up at the airport.
**Neither** the manager **nor** the other employees **were** told about the closure.
**Either** you **or** Jake **has** to stay with Grandma tonight.

drill.sentence: Neither the coach nor the players {{want}} to talk to reporters after the loss.
drill.hint: Make the verb agree with the closer subject: Neither the coach nor the players ___ (want) to talk to reporters after the loss.

mistake.wrong: Either the kids or their mother are going to call you.
mistake.right: Either the kids or their mother is going to call you.
mistake.why: In careful writing, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, *their mother*; or reverse the order and use *are*.

entries.term: data and media as singular (US)
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In most American usage, *data* is treated as a singular mass noun (*The data is clear*), and *the media* often takes a singular verb too; *data are* survives mainly in formal science writing.
entries.usage: News, business and tech writing mostly use *data is*, while many scientific journals and APA style keep *data are*. Either way, *data* has no *-s* plural and no *a*: one item is *a data point*. *The media* can take either verb; the singular is common when it means the press as one institution.
entries.pattern: the data is / shows (common US) / the data are / show (formal science); the media is / are
examples: **The sales data shows** a big jump every December.
**The data are** consistent with a small effect, but the sample is too small to be sure.
**The media has** been camped outside the courthouse all week.

drill.sentence: The data from my fitness tracker {{suggests}} that I sleep only six hours a night.
drill.hint: Use the common American singular: The data from my fitness tracker ___ (suggest) that I sleep only six hours a night.

mistake.wrong: We collected a lot of datas.
mistake.right: We collected a lot of data.
mistake.why: *Data* is already plural in origin and never takes *-s*; for one item, say *a data point*.

entries.term: classical plurals: criteria, phenomena, hypotheses
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Some Greek and Latin nouns keep their classical plurals: *criterion → criteria*, *phenomenon → phenomena*, *hypothesis → hypotheses*, *analysis → analyses*.
entries.usage: The classical forms are standard in formal and academic writing, and *a criteria* or *this phenomena* is a common error, even among native speakers. *Criteria* used as a singular is heard in speech, but careful listeners notice it. Plurals in *-ses* end in a *seez* sound (*analyses*, *crises*).
entries.pattern: criterion / criteria, phenomenon / phenomena, hypothesis / hypotheses, analysis / analyses
examples: The main **criterion** for the scholarship is financial need.
The northern lights are one of the natural **phenomena** that bring tourists to Iceland in winter.
Doctors tested several **hypotheses** before finding the cause of her fever.

drill.sentence: Price was the only {{criterion}} we used to pick the hotel.
drill.hint: Use the correct singular: Price was the only criteria we used to pick the hotel.

mistake.wrong: This phenomena is common in big cities.
mistake.right: This phenomenon is common in big cities.
mistake.why: *Phenomena* is the plural; the singular is *phenomenon*.

entries.term: plural-looking singulars: news, politics, economics
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Some nouns end in *-s* but take a singular verb: *news*, subject names like *economics, physics* and *mathematics*, and sports like *gymnastics*.
entries.usage: *News* is uncountable: *The news is good*, never *the news are*, and one item is *a piece of news*. *Politics* is singular as a field (*Politics is a tough business*) but usually plural when it means someone's views (*His politics are hard to pin down*). *Statistics* works the same way: singular as a subject, plural for the numbers.
entries.pattern: news / economics / physics / gymnastics + singular verb
examples: **The news is** on at six if you want to catch the weather.
**Economics was** my favorite class in my first year of college.
**Gymnastics is** one of the hardest sports to judge fairly.

drill.sentence: I'm afraid the news from the vet {{isn't}} very good.
drill.hint: Choose isn't or aren't: I'm afraid the news from the vet ___ very good.

mistake.wrong: The news are really bad today.
mistake.right: The news is really bad today.
mistake.why: *News* is uncountable and always takes a singular verb.

entries.term: amounts as singular: Ten dollars is …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A plural amount of money, time, distance or weight takes a singular verb when it is seen as one sum: *Ten dollars is too much for a coffee.*
entries.usage: Normal in all registers: *Three weeks is a long time*, *Five miles is too far to walk*. A plural verb is used when you think of the separate units, especially with *the last* or *the past* (*The last three weeks have been crazy*).
entries.pattern: plural amount (money / time / distance / weight) + singular verb
examples: **Fifteen dollars is** way too much for a sandwich.
**Two hours is** a long time to sit in a waiting room with a sick kid.
**Ten pounds is** a lot to lose in a month.

drill.sentence: Three hundred dollars {{seems}} like a lot for a pair of sneakers.
drill.hint: Choose seem or seems: Three hundred dollars ___ like a lot for a pair of sneakers.

mistake.wrong: Twenty dollars are enough for the taxi.
mistake.right: Twenty dollars is enough for the taxi.
mistake.why: The amount is treated as one sum, so the verb is singular.

entries.term: along with / as well as: the verb agrees with the first subject
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Phrases added with *along with, as well as, together with* or *in addition to* do not make the subject plural; the verb agrees with the first noun: *The CEO, along with two managers, is …*
entries.usage: Common in news and formal writing, where the added phrase is often between commas. If you want a plural verb, use *and* (*The CEO and two managers are …*). In casual speech, people often use a plural verb anyway, but editors treat that as an error.
entries.pattern: subject + (along with / as well as / together with + noun) + verb agreeing with the subject
examples: My sister, **along with** her three kids, **is** staying with us for the holidays.
The coach, **as well as** several players, **has** been suspended for the next game.
The price, **together with** shipping, **comes** to just under a hundred dollars.

drill.sentence: The mayor, along with two council members, {{plans}} to attend the opening.
drill.hint: Make the verb agree with the first subject: The mayor, along with two council members, ___ (plan) to attend the opening.

mistake.wrong: The teacher, as well as the students, were surprised.
mistake.right: The teacher, as well as the students, was surprised.
mistake.why: In careful writing, *as well as* does not make the subject plural, so the verb agrees with *the teacher*.

entries.term: the majority of + plural verb
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: With *the majority of* + plural noun, the verb is plural because it agrees with the noun after *of*: *The majority of voters are …*
entries.usage: Common in news, surveys and reports. *The majority* alone can take either verb; the singular treats the group as one body (*The majority has spoken*). With uncountable nouns, *most of* sounds more natural than *the majority of* (*most of the work*).
entries.pattern: the majority of + plural noun + plural verb / the majority (alone) + singular or plural verb
examples: **The majority of** our customers **are** repeat buyers.
**The majority of** the kids in my son's class **walk** to school.
**The vast majority of** residents **want** the old theater to be restored.

drill.sentence: The majority of the apartments in this building {{have}} balconies.
drill.hint: Choose has or have: The majority of the apartments in this building ___ balconies.

mistake.wrong: The majority of people thinks the new park is a good idea.
mistake.right: The majority of people think the new park is a good idea.
mistake.why: The verb agrees with *people*, the noun after *of*, so it is plural.

entries.term: percentages and fractions: 60% of people are …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: With percentages and fractions + *of*, the verb agrees with the noun after *of*: *60 percent of people are …*, but *60 percent of the money is …*
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and presentations: a plural noun takes a plural verb, and an uncountable or singular noun takes a singular verb (*Half of the cake was gone*). *The percentage of* takes a singular verb, like *the number of*. American English usually writes *percent* as one word.
entries.pattern: percentage / fraction + of + noun → the verb agrees with that noun
examples: About **70 percent of** the houses in our neighborhood **were** built before 1950.
**Half of** the pizza **was** gone before I even got to the party.
**Two-thirds of** the students **were** out sick on Friday.

drill.sentence: Forty percent of the budget {{goes}} to salaries.
drill.hint: Choose go or goes: Forty percent of the budget ___ to salaries.

mistake.wrong: Half of the cookies is gone.
mistake.right: Half of the cookies are gone.
mistake.why: The verb agrees with *cookies*, the noun after *of*.

entries.term: a great deal of vs. a great many
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *A great deal of* + uncountable noun means *a large amount of*; *a great many* + plural noun, with no *of*, means *a large number of*.
entries.usage: Both sound formal or slightly old-fashioned; in speech, *a lot of* is far more common. *A great many* takes *of* only before a determiner or pronoun (*a great many of them*). *A great deal* also works as an adverb (*She travels a great deal*).
entries.pattern: a great deal of + uncountable noun / a great many + plural noun
examples: Raising twins takes **a great deal of** patience.
**A great many** families lost their homes in the flood.
She has traveled **a great deal** since she retired.

drill.sentence: {{A great many}} visitors have complained about the parking.
drill.hint: Make it formal (plural noun): Many visitors have complained about the parking.

mistake.wrong: A great deal of people came to the funeral.
mistake.right: A great many people came to the funeral.
mistake.why: *A great deal of* is only for uncountable nouns; with plural nouns, use *a great many* or *a lot of*.

entries.term: few vs. a few
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Few* + plural noun means *not many*, with a negative feel (*Few people came*); *a few* means *some, a small number*, with a positive or neutral feel.
entries.usage: *Few* alone sounds formal; in speech, people say *not many* or *very few*. *Only a few* is negative in meaning, like *few*, while *quite a few* means *many*. The choice changes the message: *I have a few friends here* is fine, but *I have few friends here* is sad.
entries.pattern: few + plural noun (= not many) / a few + plural noun (= some)
examples: **Few** people know that she wrote the song herself.
I've already made **a few** friends at my new gym.
**Very few** tourists know about the little beach behind the lighthouse.

drill.sentence: I still have {{a few}} questions about the lease before I sign it.
drill.hint: Positive meaning (some): I still have ___ questions about the lease before I sign it.

mistake.wrong: I have few friends here, so I'm never lonely.
mistake.right: I have a few friends here, so I'm never lonely.
mistake.why: *Few* sounds negative (not enough); *a few* means some.

entries.term: little vs. a little
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Little* + uncountable noun means *not much*, with a negative feel (*There's little hope*); *a little* means *some, a small amount*, with a positive or neutral feel.
entries.usage: *Little* in this sense sounds formal or written; in speech, people say *not much* or *very little*. Do not confuse it with *little* meaning *small* (*a little house*). *A little* also works as an adverb before adjectives and comparatives (*a little tired*, *a little more*).
entries.pattern: little + uncountable noun (= not much) / a little + uncountable noun (= some)
examples: There's **little** chance of rain this weekend, so let's plan the picnic.
Could you add **a little** more milk to my coffee?
He showed **very little** interest in taking over the family business.

drill.sentence: Unfortunately, there's {{little}} we can do until the insurance company calls back.
drill.hint: Negative meaning, one word (not much): Unfortunately, there's ___ we can do until the insurance company calls back.

mistake.wrong: Sadly, there's a little chance he'll be ready for the final.
mistake.right: Sadly, there's little chance he'll be ready for the final.
mistake.why: *A little* means some; for the negative idea *not much*, drop *a*.

entries.term: whom in formal English: to whom, for whom
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Whom* is the object form of *who*; formal English uses it after prepositions (*to whom, for whom, with whom*) and as the object in a relative clause.
entries.usage: In everyday American speech, *whom* is fading: people say *Who did you talk to?* and *the woman I met*. It survives in formal letters, legal and academic writing and fixed phrases (*To whom it may concern*). Directly after a preposition, *whom* is still required (*with whom*, not *with who*).
entries.pattern: preposition + whom / whom as object (formal); who … + preposition at the end (everyday)
examples: She married a man **whom** she had met only twice.
I'd like to thank the colleagues **with whom** I worked most closely.
The award goes to a teacher **for whom** no student was ever a lost cause.

drill.sentence: {{To whom}} should I address the letter?
drill.hint: Make it formal: Who should I address the letter to?

mistake.wrong: Whom is calling, please?
mistake.right: Who is calling, please?
mistake.why: *Whom* is only an object; as the subject of a verb, use *who*.

entries.term: whose for things: a company whose profits …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Whose* can refer to things as well as people: *a company whose profits fell*, *a house whose roof leaks*.
entries.usage: Normal in all registers, and much smoother than *of which* (*a house the roof of which leaks* sounds very formal). Some learners believe *whose* is only for people and build awkward sentences to avoid it. Don't confuse it with *who's* (= *who is* or *who has*), which sounds the same.
entries.pattern: noun (thing or person) + whose + noun + verb
examples: We stayed in an old hotel **whose** elevator broke down twice a day.
It's one of those bands **whose** songs everyone knows but nobody can name.
Investors are pulling out of companies **whose** profits depend on a single product.

drill.sentence: I bought a used car {{whose}} previous owner was a mechanic.
drill.hint: Join with a relative clause: I bought a used car. Its previous owner was a mechanic.

mistake.wrong: It's a company who's profits keep falling.
mistake.right: It's a company whose profits keep falling.
mistake.why: *Who's* means *who is* or *who has*; the possessive relative word is *whose*.

entries.term: all vs. whole: the whole day / all day
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Whole* goes with singular countable nouns and comes after *the, a* or *my* (*the whole day*, *my whole life*); *all* comes before *the* or *my* and goes with plurals, uncountables and time words (*all day*, *all the money*, *all my friends*).
entries.usage: For time, *all day*, *all week* and *the whole day* mean the same. With uncountable nouns, use *all* (*all the money*, not *the whole money*). *Whole* + plural noun means complete units (*Whole families were evacuated*), which is different from *all*.
entries.pattern: the / a / my + whole + singular noun / all (the / my) + uncountable or plural noun
examples: I spent **the whole day** cleaning out the garage.
It rained **all week**, so the kids were bouncing off the walls.
She ate **the whole pizza** by herself in one sitting.

drill.sentence: I've lived in Ohio {{my whole life}}, and I've never seen a tornado.
drill.hint: Rewrite with whole: I've lived in Ohio all my life, and I've never seen a tornado.

mistake.wrong: He spent the whole money on a new TV.
mistake.right: He spent all the money on a new TV.
mistake.why: *Whole* is for singular countable nouns; with an uncountable noun like *money*, use *all*.

entries.term: hyphenated compound adjectives: a well-known author / she is well known
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A compound adjective is hyphenated before a noun (*a well-known author*), but after a verb the hyphen is often dropped (*She is well known*).
entries.usage: The hyphen before a noun shows that the words form one modifier. After a verb, style guides differ: Chicago style drops the hyphen (*well known*), while AP style and many dictionaries keep it (*well-known*). Adverbs ending in *-ly* never take a hyphen (*a highly paid job*).
entries.pattern: well-known / up-to-date / long-term + noun; be + well known / up to date
examples: Her mother is a **well-known** author of children's books.
Make sure your passport is **up to date** before you book the trip.
We're looking for a **long-term** solution, not a quick fix.

drill.sentence: It's a {{family-owned}} restaurant that's been around since 1952.
drill.hint: Put the compound adjective before the noun: The restaurant is owned by a family and has been around since 1952.

mistake.wrong: She has a highly-paid job in finance.
mistake.right: She has a highly paid job in finance.
mistake.why: AP, Chicago and other major style guides never hyphenate after an *-ly* adverb, because the *-ly* already shows how the words connect.

entries.term: noun + noun vs. 's vs. of: the car door, the company's success
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: English uses a noun modifier for types and fixed combinations (*the car door*, *a coffee cup*), *'s* for owners, people and organizations (*the company's success*), and *of* for parts of things and long phrases (*the end of the movie*).
entries.usage: *'s* is most natural with people, animals, organizations, places and time (*Sarah's car*, *the city's budget*, *today's news*); *of* is preferred with things and long noun phrases (*the top of the page*). A noun modifier names a type, not an owner: *a coffee cup* is for coffee, while *a cup of coffee* has coffee in it.
entries.pattern: noun + noun (type) / owner + 's + noun / the + part + of + thing
examples: The **car door** hasn't closed properly since the accident.
**The company's success** surprised everyone, including its founders.
I always fall asleep before **the end of the movie**.

drill.sentence: I really value {{my mother's opinion}} on big decisions.
drill.hint: Use the most natural possessive form: I really value the opinion of my mother on big decisions.

mistake.wrong: We stayed at the house of my parents for a week.
mistake.right: We stayed at my parents' house for a week.
mistake.why: With people as owners, English uses *'s* (or *s'*); *the house of my parents* sounds translated.

entries.term: double possessive: a friend of mine
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *A, an, this* or *that* + noun + *of* + possessive (*mine, yours, Sarah's*) means one of several, or adds feeling: *a friend of mine*, *that dog of yours*.
entries.usage: Normal in all registers, and needed because *a* and *my* cannot stand together (*a my friend* is impossible). *A friend of mine* presents someone new, while *my friend* suggests someone the listener already knows about. With *this* or *that*, it often sounds emotional or critical (*that brother of yours*).
entries.pattern: a / an / this / that + noun + of + mine / yours / his / hers / ours / theirs / name's
examples: **A friend of mine** runs a bakery downtown; you should try her croissants.
Is that **a cousin of yours**? He looks just like you.
**That dog of theirs** barks every time someone walks by.

drill.sentence: {{A colleague of mine}} recommended this dentist, and she's great.
drill.hint: Rewrite with a double possessive: One of my colleagues recommended this dentist, and she's great.

mistake.wrong: She's a friend of me from college.
mistake.right: She's a friend of mine from college.
mistake.why: In this pattern, *of* is followed by the possessive pronoun *mine*, not *me*.

entries.term: time possessive: a week's notice, two years' experience
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *'s* (singular) or *s'* (plural) after a time noun expresses a length of time: *a week's notice*, *two years' experience*, *a day's work*.
entries.usage: Common in job ads, contracts and everyday speech (*an hour's drive*, *a good night's sleep*). For plurals, the apostrophe goes after the *s* (*three months' rent*). American English often uses *of* with experience instead (*five years of experience*), and casual writing sometimes drops the apostrophe.
entries.pattern: a + time noun + 's + noun / number + plural time noun + s' + noun
examples: I gave my boss **two weeks' notice** on Monday.
The cabin is about **an hour's drive** from Denver.
There's nothing like **a good night's sleep** before a big game.

drill.sentence: The landlord wants {{three months'}} rent as a security deposit.
drill.hint: Rewrite with a time possessive: The landlord wants rent for three months as a security deposit.

mistake.wrong: She has five year's experience in sales.
mistake.right: She has five years' experience in sales.
mistake.why: With a plural time noun, the apostrophe goes after the *s*: *years'*.

entries.term: than me vs. than I (am)
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After *than* and *as*, an object pronoun is normal in everyday English (*She's taller than me*); a subject pronoun followed by a verb is the careful form (*She's taller than I am*).
entries.usage: *Than me* is standard in speech and informal writing. *Than I* with no verb (*taller than I*) sounds stiff to most Americans, so *than I am* is the safe choice in formal writing. Sometimes it matters: *She likes you more than I do* is clear, while *She likes you more than me* can also mean *more than she likes me*.
entries.pattern: than / as + me / him / her (everyday) / than / as + I am / he does (careful)
examples: My little brother is already taller **than me**.
She's been at the company longer **than I have**.
Nobody loves this town as much **as he does**.

drill.sentence: My sister earns a lot more {{than I do}}, but she works twice as hard.
drill.hint: Make it careful style, with a verb: My sister earns a lot more than me, but she works twice as hard.

mistake.wrong: He runs much faster than I am.
mistake.right: He runs much faster than I do.
mistake.why: The verb after *than* must match the first verb: *runs* → *I do*, *is taller* → *I am*.

entries.term: misused myself: Contact John or myself
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Myself* is reflexive (*I hurt myself*) or emphatic (*I did it myself*); it needs *I* as the subject of the same clause and is not a polite replacement for *me*.
entries.usage: *Please contact John or myself* and *John and myself will attend* are very common in business English, even among native speakers, because *myself* feels more formal. Many editors and careful listeners treat it as an error. Use *me* as an object and *I* as a subject.
entries.pattern: I + verb + myself (reflexive) / I … myself (emphasis); otherwise me / I
examples: I cut **myself** while I was chopping onions last night.
I built the whole deck **myself**, and it only took two weekends.
If you have any questions, contact Lisa or **me** directly.

drill.sentence: Please contact {{me}} directly if the package doesn't arrive.
drill.hint: Correct the pronoun: Please contact myself directly if the package doesn't arrive.

mistake.wrong: Please send the documents to John or myself.
mistake.right: Please send the documents to John or me.
mistake.why: *Myself* needs *I* as the subject in the same clause; otherwise use *me*.

entries.term: the with geographic names: the Netherlands, the Alps
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Most country, city, lake and single-mountain names take no article, but plural names, rivers, oceans, seas, mountain ranges and names with *Republic, Kingdom* or *States* take *the*: *the Netherlands, the Alps, the Amazon, the United States*.
entries.usage: Single places with a simple proper name have no article (*Canada, Lake Tahoe, Mount Rainier*). Plural names and names that contain a common noun like *republic* or *kingdom* take *the* (*the Philippines, the Dominican Republic*). Rivers take *the* even though lakes do not (*the Mississippi* vs. *Lake Michigan*).
entries.pattern: the + plural names / rivers / oceans / seas / mountain ranges / Republic, Kingdom, States
examples: We spent two weeks hiking in **the Rockies** last summer.
She grew up in **the Netherlands** but moved to **Canada** at sixteen.
The town sits right on **the Mississippi**, so it floods every few years.

drill.sentence: My grandparents crossed {{the Atlantic}} by ship in 1956.
drill.hint: Add the if needed: My grandparents crossed ___ (Atlantic) by ship in 1956.

mistake.wrong: My parents live in Philippines.
mistake.right: My parents live in the Philippines.
mistake.why: Plural country names take *the*: *the Philippines*, *the Netherlands*, *the United States*.

entries.term: institution nouns: in the hospital (US), go to college
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: American English says *in the hospital*, with *the*, but uses no article with *college, school, class, jail* and *bed* when you mean their normal purpose: *go to college*, *be in school*.
entries.usage: British English says *in hospital* and *go to university*; Americans say *in the hospital* and *go to college*, where *college* means any university-level study. Use *the* when you mean the building itself, visited for another reason (*I picked her up at the school*).
entries.pattern: in the hospital (US) / go to college / be in school / go to bed / be in jail
examples: My dad's **in the hospital** after a minor heart attack, but he's doing fine.
Our daughter starts **college** in Michigan this fall.
The kids are **in school** until three, so I have the afternoon free.

drill.sentence: After the accident, she was in {{the}} hospital for a week.
drill.hint: Say it the American way: After the accident, she was in hospital for a week.

mistake.wrong: I'm tired, so I'm going to the bed now.
mistake.right: I'm tired, so I'm going to bed now.
mistake.why: Used for its normal purpose, *bed* takes no article, like *school*, *college* and *class*.

entries.term: adjective + a + noun after so / too / how: too big a risk
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After *so, too, as* and *how*, the adjective comes before *a/an*: *too big a risk*, *so good a deal*, *as strong a team as*.
entries.usage: *Too* and *how* + adjective + *a* are normal in speech and writing (*How big a problem is it?*), while *so* + adjective + *a* sounds formal and speech prefers *such a* (*such a good deal*). *Too big of a risk* is very common in American speech, but editors remove the *of* in writing. It works only with *a / an* + a singular countable noun.
entries.pattern: so / too / as / how + adjective + a / an + noun
examples: Quitting without another job lined up was **too big a risk** for us.
It wasn't **as bad a winter as** everyone had predicted.
**How big a tip** should we leave for a table of twelve?

drill.sentence: That's {{too important a decision}} to make in a hurry.
drill.hint: Rewrite with too + adjective + a: That decision is too important to make in a hurry.

mistake.wrong: It's a too big risk.
mistake.right: It's too big a risk.
mistake.why: After *too*, the adjective comes before *a*.

entries.term: quite a + noun: That's quite a story
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Quite a / an* + noun means a remarkable, unusual or impressive example of something: *That's quite a story* means *that's a remarkable story*.
entries.usage: Informal and very common in speech, often as a reaction (*That was quite a game!*). It can be admiring or slightly ironic, depending on the tone. With an adjective, the meaning is weaker: *quite a long time* means *a fairly long time*.
entries.pattern: quite a / an + noun (= a remarkable …)
examples: Running a marathon at seventy is **quite an achievement**.
Wow, that's **quite a view** from your balcony.
She's **quite a character**; everyone in town knows her.

drill.sentence: Ten inches of snow overnight? That was {{quite a storm}}.
drill.hint: React with quite: That was a remarkable storm.

mistake.wrong: That's a quite story.
mistake.right: That's quite a story.
mistake.why: *Quite* comes before *a*, not after it.

entries.term: kind of / sort of agreement: these kinds of things
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In careful English, the demonstrative matches *kind* or *sort*: *this kind of problem* (singular), *these kinds of problems* (plural).
entries.usage: *These kind of things* is very common in American speech, even from educated speakers, but editors correct it in writing. Use *this kind of* + singular or uncountable noun, and *these kinds of* + plural noun. *Kind of* as an informal adverb (*kind of tired* = a bit tired) is a different use.
entries.pattern: this / that kind of + noun / these / those kinds of + plural noun
examples: I love **these kinds of** small, family-run restaurants.
**This kind of** weather always gives me a headache.
We don't usually get **those kinds of** questions from customers.

drill.sentence: {{These kinds of mistakes are}} easy to avoid if you use a checklist.
drill.hint: Make it plural: This kind of mistake is easy to avoid if you use a checklist.

mistake.wrong: I don't really like these kind of movies.
mistake.right: I don't really like these kinds of movies.
mistake.why: In writing, *these* needs a plural noun (*these kinds*); or keep everything singular (*this kind of movie*).

entries.term: any (= no matter which): Any student can …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Stressed *any* in a positive sentence means *every one, no matter which*: *Any student can join* means every student, without exception.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing; in speech, *any* is stressed (*ANY doctor will tell you that*). It is usually followed by a singular countable or an uncountable noun, and it differs from unstressed *any* in questions and negatives (*Do you have any questions?*). *Anyone, anything* and *any time* work the same way.
entries.pattern: any + singular noun (stressed) = every one, no matter which
examples: **Any** doctor will tell you that sleep matters as much as exercise.
Come by **any time**; we're home all weekend.
**Any** kid in the neighborhood can join the summer league for free.

drill.sentence: {{Any pharmacy}} can fill this prescription, so don't drive across town.
drill.hint: Say it with any: Every pharmacy, no matter which one, can fill this prescription, so don't drive across town.

mistake.wrong: Any student can't enter the building after nine.
mistake.right: No student can enter the building after nine.
mistake.why: *Any* cannot be the subject of a negative verb; use *no* + noun instead.
